title: The golden goose
hookLine: a golden bird gives one feather at a time; the greedy wife plucks it bare and the gold turns ordinary (Jataka 136)

lines: NOT THE GOOSE WITH THE EGGS.
A FATHER REBORN AS A GOLDEN GOOSE.
cards: You've probably heard of the goose that laid golden eggs: the farmer cut it open to get all the gold at once, and got nothing. That's Aesop. The Jataka has a cousin of it, stranger and sadder.

A good man dies and leaves a wife and three daughters with almost nothing. He's reborn, tradition says, as a goose with feathers of pure gold, and one day he remembers his old life and the family he left.
He flies to find them, living poor, working for other people, and lands on their roof.

teach.h: ONE GOLDEN FEATHER AT A TIME.
teach.b: The family is frightened at first. Then the goose tells them who he is. I was your husband, your father.
I've come to help. Each time I come, I'll leave you one of my golden feathers. And he does.
They sell the feathers, and little by little life gets easier: food, a little comfort. Then the mother starts thinking. Birds can't be trusted, she tells her daughters.
One day he'll just stop coming.
Next time, let's pluck him bare and get all the gold at once. The daughters refuse: that would hurt him. But the next time the goose comes, the mother grabs him and pulls out every feather.
And the gold turns ordinary: plain feathers, no better than a crane's.

The story says only that they were plucked against his will; some readers take the point to be that the gold was his to give, and taken by force, it was gold no more. His wings are bare. He can't fly.
They put him in a big jar and feed him, and in time his feathers grow back, plain white.
When he can fly again, he flies away, and never comes back.
The verse at the end of the Jataka says something like: be content with what you're given; greed loses even the gold you had. Notice the shape of it. No punishment from outside.
The gift simply couldn't survive being grabbed. One feather at a time, freely given, was more than enough.

how: Buddhist teachers use the golden goose story to teach contentment (santutthi), and the Jataka's frame story ties it to a monastic rule about taking more than was offered.

o: a golden egg from Aesop's fable
a golden feather given as a gift
a goose or swan, a noble bird

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: this is the same story as Aesop's goose with golden eggs
a cousin, not a copy: here a reborn father gives his own feathers.
the plucked feathers stopped being gold
taken by force, they turned plain.
the goose came back once his feathers grew in
they grew back white, and he flew away for good.

games.q: you're one of the daughters. your mother wants to pluck the golden goose bare, to get all the gold at once. what do you say?
o: yes, let's do it before he stops coming.
games.why: the daughters refuse. the mother does it anyway, and the gold turns ordinary.

practice: Something good in your life may come a little at a time: a friendship, rest, a person's patience, money, maybe. Notice any part of you that wants to grab it all, now, just in case, and feel the grip.
Then, on an out-breath, loosen it; one feather at a time is enough.

wordCard.voice: Hamsa. The golden goose: a father reborn as this bird, giving one feather at a time, until greed plucked him bare and the gold turned ordinary.

orig.note: Pali: a goose or swan, a noble bird in Indian stories. The story is the Suvannahamsa Jataka, the golden goose.

carryVoice: Your line: greed plucks the goose bare. The daughters said no; the mother grabbed. Ninety days, just like that.
